en.content: 1 mole of an ideal gas is expanded from an initial pressure of 1 bar to final pressure of 0.1 bar at constant temperature of 0°C. Identify the incorrect one for the process
en.explanation:
For an ideal gas, internal energy and enthalpy depend only on temperature.

Here the gas is expanded at constant temperature, from $1 \text{ bar}$ to $0.1 \text{ bar}$.

Since temperature is constant,

$$ \Delta U = 0 $$

So option A is correct.

Also, for an ideal gas,

$$ H = U + PV $$

and $H$ also depends only on temperature. Since temperature does not change,

$$ \Delta H = 0 $$

So option C is correct.

Now, from the ideal gas equation,

$$ PV = nRT $$

Here $n = 1$ mole and $T$ is constant. So $PV$ remains constant.

$$ \Delta(PV) = 0 $$

So option D is also correct.

But entropy changes during isothermal expansion. For an ideal gas,

$$ \Delta S = nR \ln \frac{V_2}{V_1} $$

At constant temperature,

$$ P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 $$

So,

$$ \frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{P_1}{P_2} $$

Given,

$$ \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{1}{0.1} = 10 $$

Thus,

$$ \Delta S = R \ln 10 $$

This is not zero.

So the incorrect statement is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option B: } \Delta S = 0} $$

en.content: Given, H2(g) + Br2(g) → 2HBr(g), $\Delta H_1^\circ$, and standard enthalpy of condensation of bromine is $\Delta H_2^\circ$, standard enthalpy of formation of HBr at 25°C is
en.explanation:
The standard enthalpy of formation of HBr is defined for the reaction where the elements are taken in their standard states. At 25°C, bromine's standard state is liquid, not gas. So we need the reaction:

$$\tfrac{1}{2} H_2(g) + \tfrac{1}{2} Br_2(l) \rightarrow HBr(g)$$

The given reaction uses $Br_2(g)$:

$$H_2(g) + Br_2(g) \rightarrow 2HBr(g), \quad \Delta H_1^\circ$$

And condensation of bromine is:

$$Br_2(g) \rightarrow Br_2(l), \quad \Delta H_2^\circ$$

To reach the formation reaction, first reverse the condensation to convert $Br_2(l)$ into $Br_2(g)$, which costs $-\Delta H_2^\circ$. Then use the given reaction to form 2 HBr, which contributes $\Delta H_1^\circ$.

So for 2 moles of HBr:

$$\Delta H = \Delta H_1^\circ - \Delta H_2^\circ$$

For 1 mole (which is what formation enthalpy needs):

$$\Delta H_f^\circ(HBr) = \frac{\Delta H_1^\circ - \Delta H_2^\circ}{2}$$

The correct option is D.

en.content: If enthalpy of dissociation of CH4 and C2H6 are 320 and 600 calories respectively then bond energy of C–C bond is :
en.explanation:
For methane, $CH_4$, there are $4$ C–H bonds.

Given enthalpy of dissociation of $CH_4 = 320$ cal.

So, bond energy of one C–H bond is

$$ \frac{320}{4} = 80 \text{ cal} $$

Now, ethane is $C_2H_6$.

Its structure has:

  • $6$ C–H bonds

  • $1$ C–C bond

Given enthalpy of dissociation of $C_2H_6 = 600$ cal.

So,

$$ 6(\text{C–H bond energy}) + \text{C–C bond energy} = 600 $$

$$ 6(80) + \text{C–C bond energy} = 600 $$

$$ 480 + \text{C–C bond energy} = 600 $$

$$ \text{C–C bond energy} = 600 - 480 = 120 \text{ cal} $$

So, the bond energy of the C–C bond is

$$ \boxed{120 \text{ cal}} $$

Correct option: D.

en.content: At 25°C and 1 atm pressure, the enthalpy of combustion of benzene (l) and acetylene (g) are $-3268~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}}$ and $-1300~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}}$, respectively. The change in enthalpy for the reaction $3\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\rightarrow \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6(\mathrm{l})$, is
en.explanation:
For acetylene combustion:

$$ \mathrm{C_2H_2(g)}+\frac{5}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO_2(g)}+\mathrm{H_2O(l)} $$

$$ \Delta H=-1300~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}} $$

For $3$ moles of acetylene:

$$ 3\mathrm{C_2H_2(g)}+\frac{15}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 6\mathrm{CO_2(g)}+3\mathrm{H_2O(l)} $$

$$ \Delta H=3(-1300)=-3900~\mathrm{kJ} $$

For benzene combustion:

$$ \mathrm{C_6H_6(l)}+\frac{15}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 6\mathrm{CO_2(g)}+3\mathrm{H_2O(l)} $$

$$ \Delta H=-3268~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}} $$

We need benzene on the product side, so reverse this reaction:

$$ 6\mathrm{CO_2(g)}+3\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6(l)}+\frac{15}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} $$

$$ \Delta H=+3268~\mathrm{kJ} $$

Now add the two reactions:

$$ 3\mathrm{C_2H_2(g)}+\frac{15}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 6\mathrm{CO_2(g)}+3\mathrm{H_2O(l)} $$

$$ 6\mathrm{CO_2(g)}+3\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6(l)}+\frac{15}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} $$

Common terms cancel, giving:

$$ 3\mathrm{C_2H_2(g)}\rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6(l)} $$

So,

$$ \Delta H=-3900+3268 $$

$$ \Delta H=-632~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}} $$

The correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option C: } -632~\mathrm{kJ~mol^{-1}}} $$

en.content:
A sample of gas is compressed from an initial volume of $2V_0$ to $V_0$ using three different processes.

First: Using reversible isothermal

Second: Using reversible adiabatic

Third: Using irreversible adiabatic under a constant external pressure, then :

Which of the following statements is correct?

options.content: Final temperature of gas will be highest at the end of third process.
Final temperature of gas will be highest at the end of second process.
Enthalpy change of sample will be highest in isothermal process. (magnitude wise)
Final pressure of gas will be highest at the end of second process.

en.explanation:
Take the gas as ideal. Let the initial temperature be $T_0$ and initial pressure be $P_0$ at volume $2V_0$.

For the reversible isothermal compression,

$$ T_f=T_0 $$

So temperature does not change.

For the reversible adiabatic compression,

$$ TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant} $$

So,

$$ T_f=T_0\left(\frac{2V_0}{V_0}\right)^{\gamma-1} $$

$$ T_f=T_0\,2^{\gamma-1} $$

Temperature rises because the gas is compressed adiabatically.

For the irreversible adiabatic compression against constant external pressure, $q=0$.

Using NCERT sign convention,

$$ \Delta U=q+w $$

Since $q=0$,

$$ \Delta U=w $$

For compression from $2V_0$ to $V_0$,

$$ w=-P_{\text{ext}}(V_f-V_i) $$

$$ w=-P_{\text{ext}}(V_0-2V_0)=P_{\text{ext}}V_0 $$

At the final equilibrium state,

$$ P_{\text{ext}}=P_f $$

So,

$$ w=P_fV_0=nRT_f $$

Also,

$$ \Delta U=nC_V(T_f-T_0) $$

Thus,

$$ nC_V(T_f-T_0)=nRT_f $$

$$ C_V(T_f-T_0)=RT_f $$

Since $R=C_P-C_V=(\gamma-1)C_V$,

$$ T_f-T_0=(\gamma-1)T_f $$

$$ T_0=(2-\gamma)T_f $$

$$ T_f=\frac{T_0}{2-\gamma} $$

For gases, $1<\gamma<2$, so this temperature is greater than the reversible adiabatic final temperature. Physically also, irreversible adiabatic compression needs more work than reversible adiabatic compression for the same change in volume, and since no heat is lost, this extra work increases the temperature more.

So the final temperature is highest in the third process.

Also, for an ideal gas, enthalpy depends only on temperature. In the isothermal process,

$$ \Delta T=0 $$

so

$$ \Delta H=0 $$

Thus option C is false.

The final pressure is also not highest in the reversible adiabatic process; it is higher in the irreversible adiabatic case.

Correct option: A.

en.content: Which of the following statements is not correct for a reversible process?

options.content: The system stays in thermodynamic equilibrium throughout the process.
The process occurs at an extremely slow rate.
At any stage, the process can be reversed by applying an infinitesimally small change in the opposite direction.
Reversible processes can be carried out in a finite time.

en.explanation:
The incorrect statement is:

$$\boxed{\text{Option D: Reversible processes may be performed in finite time.}}$$

In a reversible process, the system passes through a continuous series of equilibrium states. So, at every stage, the system must remain in thermodynamic equilibrium.

That is why a reversible process has to be carried out extremely slowly. If it is done quickly, finite differences in pressure, temperature, etc., will appear, and the process will become irreversible.

Also, a reversible process can be reversed at any stage by making only an infinitesimally small change in the opposite direction. This means the driving force is almost zero.

So:

  • Option A is correct.

  • Option B is correct.

  • Option C is correct.

  • Option D is incorrect.

A truly reversible process is an ideal process and would take infinite time, not finite time.

en.content: An ideal gas sample of five moles undergoes a reversible isothermal expansion at $27^{\circ}$C, with its pressure changing from 100 atm to 1 atm. Calculate the work done by the gas (ln100 = 4.6)
en.explanation:
For an ideal gas expanding isothermally and reversibly, the work done by the gas is

$$ W = nRT \ln \frac{V_2}{V_1} $$

Since the temperature is constant, for an ideal gas,

$$ P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 $$

So,

$$ \frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{P_1}{P_2} $$

Hence,

$$ W = nRT \ln \frac{P_1}{P_2} $$

Given:

$$ n = 5 $$

$$ T = 27^\circ C = 300 \, K $$

$$ P_1 = 100 \, atm $$

$$ P_2 = 1 \, atm $$

$$ \ln 100 = 4.6 $$

Using $R = 2 \, cal \, mol^{-1} K^{-1}$,

$$ W = 5 \times 2 \times 300 \times 4.6 $$

$$ W = 13800 \, cal $$

So, the work done by the gas is

$$ \boxed{13,800 \, cal} $$

Correct option: D.

en.content: One mole of monoatomic ideal gas at T K is expanded from 1 L to 2 L adiabatically under a constant external pressure of 1 atm. The final temperature of the gas in Kelvin is
en.explanation:
For an adiabatic process,

$$q=0$$

Using the first law of thermodynamics,

$$\Delta U = q+w$$

So,

$$\Delta U=w$$

The gas expands against a constant external pressure of $1\ \text{atm}$ from $1\ \text{L}$ to $2\ \text{L}$.

So the work done is

$$w=-P_{\text{ext}}(V_2-V_1)$$

$$w=-1(2-1)$$

$$w=-1\ \text{L atm}$$

For one mole of a monoatomic ideal gas,

$$\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T$$

For monoatomic gas,

$$C_V=\frac{3}{2}R$$

So,

$$\Delta U=\frac{3}{2}R(T_f-T)$$

Since $\Delta U=w$,

$$\frac{3}{2}R(T_f-T)=-1$$

Using $R=0.0821\ \text{L atm mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$,

$$\frac{3}{2}(0.0821)(T_f-T)=-1$$

$$T_f-T=-\frac{2}{3\times 0.0821}$$

$$T_f=T-\frac{2}{3\times 0.0821}$$

So the final temperature is

$$\boxed{T-\frac{2}{3\times 0.0821}}$$

Correct option: C.

en.content: For an ideal gas, the expression in adiabatic process is $T = K V^{-2/5}$. The gas may be
en.explanation:
For an ideal gas in an adiabatic process,

$$ TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant} $$

So we can write it as

$$ T = K V^{-(\gamma-1)} $$

Given expression is

$$ T = K V^{-2/5} $$

Comparing the powers of $V$,

$$ \gamma - 1 = \frac{2}{5} $$

So,

$$ \gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{5} = \frac{7}{5} $$

Now, $\gamma = \frac{7}{5}$ is the value for a diatomic gas at ordinary temperature.

Among the given gases:

  • He and Ne are monoatomic gases, so $\gamma = \frac{5}{3}$

  • $O_2$ is a diatomic gas, so $\gamma = \frac{7}{5}$

  • $NH_3$ is polyatomic

Hence, the gas may be

$$ \boxed{O_2} $$

Correct option: C.

en.content:
1 mol of monoatomic ideal gas at 300 K expands from 1 L to 8 L in two different processes

Process I : Reversible adiabatic expansion

Process II : Irreversible adiabatic expansion against the constant external pressure of 1 atm (given 1 atm L = 101 J)

Select the correct statement.

options.content: Change in internal energy in process II is less than change in internal energy of process I (Only magnitude)

en.explanation:
Process I: Reversible Adiabatic Expansion

For a reversible adiabatic process, the relationship between temperature and volume is given by:

$$T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1} = T_2 V_2^{\gamma-1}$$

Using the given initial state ($T_1 = 300 \text{ K}$, $V_1 = 1 \text{ L}$) and final volume ($V_2 = 8 \text{ L}$):

$$300 \times (1)^{\frac{5}{3} - 1} = T_{f,\text{I}} \times (8)^{\frac{5}{3} - 1}$$

$$300 \times 1 = T_{f,\text{I}} \times 8^{2/3}$$

Since $8^{2/3} = (2^3)^{2/3} = 2^2 = 4$, we get:

$$300 = T_{f,\text{I}} \times 4 \implies T_{f,\text{I}} = 75 \text{ K}$$

In an adiabatic process, there is no heat exchange ($q = 0$). By the first law of thermodynamics, the work done equals the change in internal energy ($W = \Delta U$).

$$\Delta U_{\text{I}} = n C_v (T_{f,\text{I}} - T_1)$$

$$\Delta U_{\text{I}} = 1 \times \left(\frac{3}{2} \times 8.314\right) \times (75 - 300)$$

$$\Delta U_{\text{I}} = 12.471 \times (-225) \approx -2806 \text{ J}$$

So, the magnitude of the change in internal energy (and the work done) for Process I is:

$$|\Delta U_{\text{I}}| = 2806 \text{ J}$$

$$|W_{\text{I}}| = 2806 \text{ J}$$

Process II: Irreversible Adiabatic Expansion

For an irreversible process against a constant external pressure, the work done is:

$$W_{\text{II}} = -P_{\text{ext}} (V_2 - V_1)$$

Using $P_{\text{ext}} = 1 \text{ atm}$:

$$W_{\text{II}} = -1 \text{ atm} \times (8 \text{ L} - 1 \text{ L}) = -7 \text{ atm L}$$

We are given that $1 \text{ atm L} = 101 \text{ J}$, so we convert the work into Joules:

$$W_{\text{II}} = -7 \times 101 \text{ J} = -707 \text{ J}$$

Again, since the process is adiabatic ($q = 0$), the change in internal energy equals the work done:

$$\Delta U_{\text{II}} = W_{\text{II}} = -707 \text{ J}$$

The magnitude of the change in internal energy for Process II is:

$$|\Delta U_{\text{II}}| = 707 \text{ J}$$

We can also quickly find the final temperature for this process using $\Delta U = n C_v (T_{f,\text{II}} - T_1)$:

$$-707 = 1 \times 12.471 \times (T_{f,\text{II}} - 300)$$

$$T_{f,\text{II}} - 300 \approx -56.7 \implies T_{f,\text{II}} \approx 243.3 \text{ K}$$

  • Option A: $|W_{\text{I}}| = 2806 \text{ J}$ and $|W_{\text{II}}| = 707 \text{ J}$. They are not equal.

  • Options B & C: $T_{f,\text{I}} = 75 \text{ K}$ and $T_{f,\text{II}} \approx 243.3 \text{ K}$. The correct relation is $|T_{f,\text{I}}| < |T_{f,\text{II}}|$. Both options are incorrect.

  • Option D: Comparing the magnitudes of internal energy changes, $|\Delta U_{\text{II}}| = 707 \text{ J}$ and $|\Delta U_{\text{I}}| = 2806 \text{ J}$. It is visibly clear that the magnitude of internal energy change in Process II is less than that of Process I.

Correct Answer:

Option D: Change in internal energy in process II is less than change in internal energy of process I (Only magnitude)

en.content: Standard heat of formation of ammonia is $-x$ kJ/mol. The heat of reaction when 28 gm of $N_2(g)$ reacted with 6 g of $H_2(g)$ at S.T.P.
en.explanation:
Standard heat of formation of ammonia means the heat change when $1$ mole of $NH_3$ is formed from its elements in their standard states.

So,

$$ \frac{1}{2}N_2(g)+\frac{3}{2}H_2(g)\rightarrow NH_3(g) $$

For formation of $1$ mole of $NH_3$,

$$ \Delta H=-x\ \text{kJ} $$

Now given:

$$ 28\text{ g of }N_2 = 1\text{ mole of }N_2 $$

and

$$ 6\text{ g of }H_2 = 3\text{ moles of }H_2 $$

The balanced reaction is:

$$ N_2(g)+3H_2(g)\rightarrow 2NH_3(g) $$

Here, $1$ mole of $N_2$ reacts with $3$ moles of $H_2$ to form $2$ moles of $NH_3$.

Since heat of formation of $1$ mole of $NH_3$ is $-x$ kJ, heat released for formation of $2$ moles of $NH_3$ is:

$$ 2(-x)=-2x\ \text{kJ} $$

So, the heat of reaction is:

$$ \boxed{-2x\ \text{kJ}} $$

Correct option: B.

en.content: Enthalpy of formation of H2O(l), CO2(g), and C6H12O6(s) at standard state is x, y, and z kJ/mol. The heat of combustion of C6H12O6(s) at standard state (in kJ/mol) is
en.explanation:
For combustion of glucose, the balanced chemical equation is

$$ \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6(s) + 6O_2(g) \rightarrow 6CO_2(g) + 6H_2O(l)} $$

The heat of reaction is found using standard enthalpies of formation:

$$ \Delta H^\circ_{\text{reaction}} = \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{reactants}) $$

Given:

$$ \Delta H_f^\circ \left(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\right) = x $$

$$ \Delta H_f^\circ \left(\mathrm{CO_2(g)}\right) = y $$

$$ \Delta H_f^\circ \left(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6(s)}\right) = z $$

Also, oxygen is in its standard elemental form, so

$$ \Delta H_f^\circ \left(\mathrm{O_2(g)}\right) = 0 $$

Now substitute:

$$ \Delta H^\circ_{\text{combustion}} = \left[6y + 6x\right] - \left[z + 6(0)\right] $$

$$ \Delta H^\circ_{\text{combustion}} = 6x + 6y - z $$

So the correct option is

en.content: At 273 K and 1 atm, one mole of ice changes to water. The entropies of H2O (s) and H2O (l) are 38.0 and 58.0 J/K-mol, respectively. The enthalpy change for this process is
en.explanation:
For the conversion of ice into water at $273\ \text{K}$:

$$ \text{H}_2\text{O}(s) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) $$

The entropy change is

$$ \Delta S = S_{\text{liquid}} - S_{\text{solid}} $$

Given,

$$ S_{\text{solid}} = 38.0\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} $$

$$ S_{\text{liquid}} = 58.0\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} $$

So,

$$ \Delta S = 58.0 - 38.0 = 20.0\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} $$

At the melting point, ice and water are in equilibrium, so

$$ \Delta G = 0 $$

Using

$$ \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S $$

we get

$$ 0 = \Delta H - T\Delta S $$

So,

$$ \Delta H = T\Delta S $$

Now substitute the values:

$$ \Delta H = 273 \times 20.0 $$

$$ \Delta H = 5460\ \text{J mol}^{-1} $$

Since melting of ice is an endothermic process, the enthalpy change is positive.

So, the correct answer is:

$$ \boxed{5460\ \text{J mol}^{-1}} $$

Option B.

en.explanation:
For a reaction to be spontaneous, Gibbs free energy should be negative:

$$ \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S $$

Now check each case.

If $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$, then

$$ \Delta G = \text{negative} - T(\text{positive}) $$

So $\Delta G$ is always negative. The reaction is always spontaneous.

If $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$, then

$$ \Delta G = \text{positive} - T(\text{negative}) = \text{positive} + \text{positive} $$

So $\Delta G$ is always positive. The reaction can never be spontaneous.

That means a spontaneous reaction is impossible when $\Delta H$ is positive and $\Delta S$ is negative.

Ethyl chloride is formed when ethene reacts with hydrogen chloride as follows

$\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4(g) + \mathrm{HCl}(g) \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Cl}(g): \Delta H = -72.3\ \mathrm{kJ}$

Find the value of $\Delta U$ (in kJ) when 70 g of ethene and 73 g of HCl are made to react at 25$^\circ$C.
en.explanation:
For the reaction

$$ \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4(g) + \mathrm{HCl}(g) \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Cl}(g) $$

given,

$$ \Delta H = -72.3\ \text{kJ} $$

We need to find $\Delta U$ at $25^\circ \text{C}$.

The relation between $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$ is

$$ \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT $$

so,

$$ \Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT $$

On the reactant side, moles of gaseous substances $= 2$

On the product side, moles of gaseous substances $= 1$

So,

$$ \Delta n_g = 1 - 2 = -1 $$

Now for one mole of reaction,

$$ \Delta U = -72.3 - (-1)\times R \times T $$

At $25^\circ\text{C} = 298\ \text{K}$ and $R = 8.314\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$,

$$ RT = 8.314 \times 298 = 2477.6\ \text{J} = 2.48\ \text{kJ} $$

So,

$$ \Delta U = -72.3 + 2.48 = -69.82\ \text{kJ} $$

This is for 1 mole of reaction.

Now check the given amounts.

Moles of ethylene:

$$ \frac{70}{28} = 2.5\ \text{mol} $$

Moles of HCl:

$$ \frac{73}{36.5} = 2.0\ \text{mol} $$

Reaction is in the ratio $1:1$, so HCl is the limiting reagent.

Hence, number of moles of reaction $= 2$.

So total $\Delta U$ is

$$ \Delta U_{\text{total}} = 2 \times (-69.82) = -139.64\ \text{kJ} $$

So the correct answer is

$$ \boxed{-139.6\ \text{kJ}} $$

Option D.

en.content: For the neutralization of a strong acid with a strong base, the enthalpy change is $-57.32$ kJ mol−1. The enthalpy of formation of water is $-285.84$ kJ mol−1. The enthalpy of formation of aqueous hydroxyl ion is
en.explanation:
For a strong acid and a strong base, the neutralization reaction is

$$ \mathrm{H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)} $$

Its enthalpy change is given as

$$ \Delta H = -57.32\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} $$

Now use enthalpy of formation relation:

$$ \Delta H = \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{products}) - \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{reactants}) $$

So,

$$ -57.32 = \Delta H_f^\circ(H_2O) - \left[\Delta H_f^\circ(H^+) + \Delta H_f^\circ(OH^-)\right] $$

We know:

$$ \Delta H_f^\circ(H_2O) = -285.84\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} $$

Also, for hydrogen ion in aqueous state,

$$ \Delta H_f^\circ(H^+) = 0 $$

Putting these values:

$$ -57.32 = -285.84 - \Delta H_f^\circ(OH^-) $$

Rearranging,

$$ \Delta H_f^\circ(OH^-) = -285.84 + 57.32 $$

$$ \Delta H_f^\circ(OH^-) = -228.52\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} $$

So the correct answer is:

$$ \boxed{-228.52\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}} $$

en.content:
Find the enthalpy of formation (in kcal/mol) of HI(g) using the data given below.

H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g): ΔH = -44.20 kcal

HCl(g) + aq → HCl(aq): ΔH = -17.31 kcal

HI(g) + aq → HI(aq): ΔH = -19.21 kcal

KOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → KCl(aq): ΔH = -13.74 kcal

KOH(aq) + HI(aq) → KI(aq): ΔH = -13.67 kcal

Cl2(g) + 2KI(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + I2(s): ΔH = -52.42 kcal
en.explanation:
We need the enthalpy of formation of $HI(g)$, that is for the reaction

$$\frac{1}{2}H_2(g)+\frac{1}{2}I_2(s)\rightarrow HI(g)$$

We will use Hess’s law and build this reaction from the given equations.

$$H_2(g)+Cl_2(g)\rightarrow 2HCl(g), \quad \Delta H=-44.20\ \text{kcal}$$

for $1$ mole of $HCl(g)$:

$$\frac{1}{2}H_2(g)+\frac{1}{2}Cl_2(g)\rightarrow HCl(g), \quad \Delta H=-22.10$$

Now convert $HCl(g)$ into $HCl(aq)$:

$$HCl(g)\rightarrow HCl(aq), \quad \Delta H=-17.31$$

Adding these two,

$$\frac{1}{2}H_2(g)+\frac{1}{2}Cl_2(g)\rightarrow HCl(aq)$$

$$\Delta H=-22.10-17.31=-39.41\ \text{kcal}$$

Now use the neutralisation reaction:

$$KOH(aq)+HCl(aq)\rightarrow KCl(aq), \quad \Delta H=-13.74$$

Reverse it:

$$KCl(aq)\rightarrow KOH(aq)+HCl(aq), \quad \Delta H=+13.74$$

Adding with the previous result, $HCl(aq)$ cancels:

$$\frac{1}{2}H_2(g)+\frac{1}{2}Cl_2(g)+KOH(aq)\rightarrow KCl(aq)$$

$$\Delta H=-39.41-13.74=-53.15\ \text{kcal}$$

Now take

$$Cl_2(g)+2KI(aq)\rightarrow 2KCl(aq)+I_2(s), \quad \Delta H=-52.42$$

Divide by $2$:

$$\frac{1}{2}Cl_2(g)+KI(aq)\rightarrow KCl(aq)+\frac{1}{2}I_2(s), \quad \Delta H=-26.21$$

Reverse it:

$$KCl(aq)+\frac{1}{2}I_2(s)\rightarrow \frac{1}{2}Cl_2(g)+KI(aq), \quad \Delta H=+26.21$$

Add this to the earlier equation:

$$\frac{1}{2}H_2(g)+KOH(aq)+\frac{1}{2}I_2(s)\rightarrow KI(aq)$$

$$\Delta H=-53.15+26.21=-26.94\ \text{kcal}$$

Now use

$$KOH(aq)+HI(aq)\rightarrow KI(aq), \quad \Delta H=-13.67$$

Reverse it:

$$KI(aq)\rightarrow KOH(aq)+HI(aq), \quad \Delta H=+13.67$$

Add:

$$\frac{1}{2}H_2(g)+\frac{1}{2}I_2(s)\rightarrow HI(aq)$$

$$\Delta H=-26.94+13.67=-13.27\ \text{kcal}$$

Now convert aqueous $HI$ to gaseous $HI$.

Given:

$$HI(g)\rightarrow HI(aq), \quad \Delta H=-19.21$$

Reverse it:

$$HI(aq)\rightarrow HI(g), \quad \Delta H=+19.21$$

Add this:

$$\frac{1}{2}H_2(g)+\frac{1}{2}I_2(s)\rightarrow HI(g)$$

$$\Delta H=-13.27+19.21=+5.94\ \text{kcal/mol}$$

So the enthalpy of formation of $HI(g)$ is

$$\boxed{+5.94\ \text{kcal/mol}}$$

Correct option: $C$

en.content: One mole of an ideal monoatomic gas expands reversibly and adiabatically from a volume of $x$ litre to 14 litre at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Then value of $x$ will be [Given, final temperature 189 K and $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{v}}=3 / 2 \mathrm{R}$ ].
en.explanation:
For a reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas,

$$ T V^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant} $$

For a monoatomic gas,

$$ C_v=\frac{3}{2}R \quad \Rightarrow \quad C_p=C_v+R=\frac{5}{2}R $$

So,

$$ \gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_v}=\frac{\frac{5}{2}R}{\frac{3}{2}R}=\frac{5}{3} $$

Now use

$$ T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1}=T_2 V_2^{\gamma-1} $$

Given:

$$ T_1=27^\circ C=300\text{ K}, \quad T_2=189\text{ K}, \quad V_2=14\text{ L} $$

and

$$ \gamma-1=\frac{5}{3}-1=\frac{2}{3} $$

So,

$$ 300 \, x^{2/3}=189 \times 14^{2/3} $$

$$ x^{2/3}=\frac{189}{300}\times 14^{2/3} $$

$$ x^{2/3}=\frac{63}{100}\times 14^{2/3} $$

$$ x=\left(\frac{189}{300}\right)^{3/2}\times 14 $$

$$ x=(0.63)^{3/2}\times 14 $$

Also,

$$ (0.63)^{3/2}=(\sqrt{0.63})^3 \approx (0.794)^3 \approx 0.5 $$

Hence,

$$ x \approx 0.5 \times 14=7 $$

So the value of $x$ is

$$ \boxed{7\text{ litre}} $$

Given for oxalic acid, heat of neutralisation is

$$ \Delta H_{\text{ionisation}}+\Delta H_{\text{neutralisation (strong acid-strong base)}}=\Delta H_{\text{neutralisation of oxalic acid}} $$

So for $1$ gram equivalent,

$$ \Delta H_{\text{ionisation}}+(-57.3)=-53.35 $$

Now the given reaction is

Oxalic acid gives $2$ moles of $\mathrm{H^+}$, so for $1$ mole of oxalic acid there are $2$ gram equivalents.

Hence total enthalpy change is

$$ \Delta H=2\times 3.95=7.9\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} $$

en.content: The chemical reaction : $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}, \Delta \mathrm{H}^{\circ}=2.8 \mathrm{~kJ}$ is spontaneous only above 400 K . Therefore $\Delta \mathrm{S}$ of reaction must be at least ( $\mathrm{JK}^{-1}$ ).
en.explanation:
For spontaneity, the condition is

$$ \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0 $$

Here, the reaction is spontaneous only above $400\ \text{K}$.

So at the limiting temperature $T = 400\ \text{K}$, we take

$$ \Delta G = 0 $$

Then,

$$ \Delta H = T\Delta S $$

Given,

$$ \Delta H = 2.8\ \text{kJ} = 2800\ \text{J} $$

So,

$$ \Delta S = \frac{\Delta H}{T} = \frac{2800}{400} = 7\ \text{J K}^{-1} $$

Since the reaction is spontaneous only above $400\ \text{K}$, $\Delta S$ must be at least

$$ 7\ \text{J K}^{-1} $$

So the answer is:

$$ \boxed{7\ \text{J K}^{-1}} $$

So, the enthalpy of solution of $\mathrm{NaCl}(s)$ is

$$ \boxed{+5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}} $$

en.content:
For KCl, the Born-Haber cycle is considered using the following data

$$ \Delta_f H^{\circ} \text { of } \mathrm{KCl}=-436.7 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} ; \Delta_{\mathrm{Sub}} H^{\circ} \text { of } K=89.2 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $$

$\Delta_{\text {Ionization }} H^{\circ}$ for $K=419.0 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$; $\Delta_{\text {Electron gain }} H^{\circ}$ for $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathrm{g})=-348.6 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$;

$$ \Delta_{\text {Bond }} H^{\circ} \text { of } \mathrm{Cl}_2=243.0 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $$

The value of the lattice enthalpy of KCl in $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ is $\_\_\_\_$ . (Nearest integer)
en.explanation:
For the Born–Haber cycle of $\mathrm{KCl}$, we write all the changes needed to form $\mathrm{KCl(s)}$ from its elements:

$$ \mathrm{K(s) + \frac{1}{2}Cl_2(g) \rightarrow KCl(s)} $$

Given,

$$ \Delta_f H^\circ = -436.7\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} $$

  1. Sublimation of potassium:

$$ \mathrm{K(s) \rightarrow K(g)} \qquad \Delta H = 89.2 $$

  1. Ionization of potassium:

$$ \mathrm{K(g) \rightarrow K^+(g) + e^-} \qquad \Delta H = 419.0 $$

  1. Dissociation of chlorine:

Since only $\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_2}$ is needed,

$$ \mathrm{\frac{1}{2}Cl_2(g) \rightarrow Cl(g)} \qquad \Delta H = \frac{243.0}{2} = 121.5 $$

  1. Electron gain by chlorine:

$$ \mathrm{Cl(g) + e^- \rightarrow Cl^-(g)} \qquad \Delta H = -348.6 $$

  1. Formation of solid crystal from gaseous ions:

$$ \mathrm{K^+(g) + Cl^-(g) \rightarrow KCl(s)} \qquad \Delta H = -U $$

Here, $U$ is the magnitude of lattice enthalpy.

Now apply Hess’s law:

$$ -436.7 = 89.2 + 419.0 + 121.5 - 348.6 - U $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ -436.7 = 281.1 - U $$

$$\Rightarrow $$$$ U = 281.1 + 436.7 = 717.8 $$

Nearest integer:

$$ \boxed{718\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}} $$

निम्नलिखित आँकड़ों का उपयोग करते हुए KCl के लिए बॉर्न-हैबर चक्र पर विचार किया जाता है

$$ \Delta_f H^{\circ} \text { of } \mathrm{KCl}=-436.7 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} ; \Delta_{\mathrm{Sub}} H^{\circ} \text { of } K=89.2 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $$

$\Delta_{\text {Ionization }} H^{\circ}$, $K=419.0 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ के लिए; \(\Delta_{\text {Electron gain }} H^{\circ}\), $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathrm{g})=-348.6 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ के लिए;

$$ \Delta_{\text {Bond }} H^{\circ} \text { of } \mathrm{Cl}_2=243.0 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $$

$\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ में KCl की जालक एन्थैल्पी का मान $\____$ है। (निकटतम पूर्णांक)
